items.title: This is a good way to understand how early we actually are in AI diffusion right…
items.summaryText:
This is a good way to understand how early we actually are in AI diffusion right now. The vast majority of people are using AI as a chatbot for simple interactions that approximate next-generation search. This is super useful but dramatically underrepresents the full capability of AI.

On the complete other end of the spectrum, agent swarms represent possibly the ultimate form factor of what agents will do inside of our workflows. Math, cyber, bio, materials science, software engineering, finance, and any other field that has valuable tasks that can be executed in parallel where compute can be applied to accelerate work all have this characteristic.

Less than a fraction of a fraction of the population uses AI in this way right now, due to a mix of the capabilities of models relative to the user's domain, the cost of doing these types of workflows today, the harnesses available to do this style of AI work, and the availability (or lack thereof) of frontier models to the general public.

There will also be a huge amount of change management necessary to get most areas of work -beyond software and AI research- to benefit from this style of agents. Companies need to upgrade their workflows, data needs to integrated and migrated into modern platforms, and companies will need to work through compliance, governance, and security frameworks to pull it off. 

But this all represents opportunity right now. A lot of this is where the applied layer of AI will really shine in the enterprise because of the domain specificity of this type of work. You can get an early sense of where things are going and the opportunity ahead by seeing through the funnel that Andrej lays out.

items.summaryZh:
这是理解我们目前处在 AI 扩散早期阶段的一个好方法。绝大多数人只是把 AI 当作聊天机器人，用于简单交互，近似下一代搜索。这非常有用，但严重低估了 AI 的完整能力。

在完全相反的一端，智能体集群（agent swarms）可能代表了智能体在我们的工作流中最终会呈现的形态。数学、网络、生物、材料科学、软件工程、金融，以及任何其他拥有可并行执行、能通过算力加速的有价值任务的领域，都具备这种特征。

目前，使用这种方式的人不到人口的一小部分中的一小部分，原因包括：模型能力与用户所在领域的匹配程度、如今执行这类工作流的成本、可用于这种 AI 工作方式的框架/工具链，以及前沿模型对公众的可用性（或缺乏可用性）。

要让软件和 AI 研究之外的大多数工作领域也能受益于这类智能体，还需要大量的变革管理。公司需要升级工作流，数据需要整合并迁移到现代平台，公司还需要处理合规、治理和安全框架才能实现。 

但这一切现在都代表着机会。由于这类工作具有领域特异性，企业级 AI 的应用层将在这里真正大放异彩。通过 Andrej 给出的这个漏斗，你可以提前感受到趋势走向和前方机会。

items.title: "I'm not at a point where I trust the agent, especially with stuff that people a…
items.summaryText:
"I'm not at a point where I trust the agent, especially with stuff that people are using."

From Micky (@Rasmic), who's taught 100K+ people to build with AI:

"The manual review is like the final step. All the work's done, and I have as much evidence from the agent as possible.

With evidence-driven testing, before and after, and even greploop, we're trying to build trust. The agent presents evidence: This is the work that's done, and this is why it's good.

For anyone who's been a developer for any time, manual review is probably the worst part of your job. This sort of helps minimize the friction."

📌 Watch Micky's full 4-step workflow here: https://t.co/ju9aMQKaCE

items.summaryText:
Day 7/

We have increased default context length for GPT-6.1 Sol to 500k when used through Codex & Work, up from 272k or an ~ 80% increase.

We will go higher in the future, but it helps reduce occurrence of compactions and with tasks that require keeping a lot of context and nuance over periods of time. It was carefully tested and is the new sweet spot for most of our users. You can still override it if you want to be higher our lower, with maximum context length of GPT-6.1 Sol of 1M.
items.summaryZh:

我们已将 GPT-6.1 Sol 通过 Codex & Work 使用时的默认上下文长度提高到 500k，高于之前的 272k，增幅约 80%。

未来我们还会继续提高，但这有助于减少压缩（compactions）的发生，也有助于处理那些需要在一段时间内保留大量上下文和细微信息的任务。我们对此进行了仔细测试，这对我们大多数用户来说是新的最佳平衡点。如果你想要更高或更低，仍然可以自行覆盖，GPT-6.1 Sol 的最大上下文长度为 1M。

items.title: Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LL…
items.summaryText:
Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.
items.summaryZh:
把这条 4 月的推文翻出来，是因为大家对 LLM 能力的共同理解之间的差距正在*扩大*。现在已经不太像“两群人各说各话”，而更像一个急剧收窄的漏斗。

- 粗略估算，大约 60 亿人（约占人口 75%）几乎完全没有接触过 LLM。
- 大约 10–20 亿人（约 20%）是免费版 ChatGPT 类产品的休闲、低频用户。这群人看到的是傻乎乎的聊天机器人，把它当成更好用的 Google 搜索、写作辅助之类的工具。也许某个智能体会试着帮你订机票。我有一些非技术圈的朋友（在我看来，合理地）说自己根本没什么用得上它的地方。甚至许多数学与代码领域之外的专业人士也处在这一层。比如，高管和许多其他职能的人大部分时间都在和别人交谈，所以虽然他们在理智上明白正在发生什么，但那仍然是二手信息，而且有点抽象。
- 现在我们来到数学与代码领域对前沿级 LLM 的专业使用。大约 2000 万人（0.2%）亲眼看到，过去需要几周/几个月才能完成的大型复杂项目，如今只需一个提示词就能由智能体完成。构建应用、复制应用、翻译应用、从二进制文件反编译应用……这一切发生得非常快、也非常近——不到 1 年前，我还在手动写代码，把记住的计算机代码命令一个字符一个字符地敲进代码编辑器，偶尔按一下 Tab 来自动补全一小段代码。
- 最后，我们来到约 5,000 人（约 0.00006%），他们能在内部使用前沿级系统。外部世界已经看到了预览。看起来像是成千上万个智能体组成的集群，在数周内协作推进软件巨型项目：铸造零日漏洞、以机器速度进行网络攻击与防御、发现新科学、推进数学前沿。这些事情过去需要行业顶尖专业人士花数年时间。与此同时，人类的审查和理解开始落后。例如，人们仍在参与几个月前 OpenAI-HF 事件的“考古”。数学家们可能还要花一段时间仔细研究那 722 篇关于前沿数学的手稿。

这个漏斗由多种因素共同驱动：
1. 影响会随着雄心、问题规模和周期而扩大。一个只需要一段话回答的问题几乎不会给系统带来压力。你需要大量你真正在意的大而困难的问题。这一方面驱动了漏斗中消费者/专业人士这一维度。
2. 系统的参差不齐（我另外写过很多关于这一点的内容）。能力在数字化、可验证且具有经济价值的领域达到峰值。这是因为 LLM 能力来自在由收入潜力驱动的精选环境混合上、基于可验证奖励的强化学习。这一方面主要驱动了漏斗中领域（例如数学与代码）这一维度。
3. 访问权限。免费层、付费层、内部。

所以这就是当下的怪异之处。公众大多没有与这些系统互动过。当他们互动时，它看起来像一个傻乎乎的聊天机器人。大多数专业人士仍然只看到适度的提升。而一小撮专业人士正在体验曲线垂直上升带来的眩晕。而这一切都在同时发生。

items.title: Frontier Chips for Frontier AI Labs, with Walter Goodwin, Founder/CEO of Fractile
items.summaryText:
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:30
Right now, we're trying to build a single chip. If you crack open an NVIDIA system, it has anywhere between kind of six and nine custom chips all built by NVIDIA to come together to build something that is really, really potent. So there's already a gap…
items.bodyText:
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:30
Right now, we're trying to build a single chip. If you crack open an NVIDIA system, it has anywhere between kind of six and nine custom chips all built by NVIDIA to come together to build something that is really, really potent. So there's already a gap there. You know, it'd be great to be productive enough that we could start to build our own responses in that same kind of way. This idea of being able to have at any given moment a kind of rolling frontier of bets that you hope are deeply aligned in which you're ready to trigger the ramp of, this is a huge advantage if you can kind of build that machine and build that engine.

Speaker 1 | 00:30 - 00:39
It's equivalent of the frontier model for the chip space is if you can just find a way to structurally carve out a three to six months advantage, you will be winning all of those deployments.

Speaker 2 | 00:46 - 01:16
Hi, listeners. Welcome back to No Priors. Today, I'm here with Walter Goodwin, founder and CEO of full stack AI chip company, Fractile. We talk about what it means to be full stack as a company, the technical bets they're making, why he's so focused on memory bandwidth, his predictions for frontier model architectures in the future, and the structure of the chip market at the frontier today and tomorrow amongst NVIDIA, AMD, internal efforts, and this new class of accelerators. Welcome, Walter.

Speaker 2 | 01:16 - 01:18
Walter, thanks so much for doing this.

Speaker 1 | 01:18 - 01:19
Very good to be here, Sarith.

Speaker 2 | 01:19 - 01:24
You started this incredibly interesting company called Fractal. Can you give us a overview of what you guys do?

Speaker 1 | 01:24 - 01:39
Fractal is a chip company. We build very, very fast inference chips for the world's largest models. This sort of bet on speed is something which we've had right from the outset. Started the company in summer of twenty twenty two. And I think at the time, we were starting to see two things.

Speaker 1 | 01:39 - 02:21
You know? One was obviously the arrival of foundation models trained on the Internet and generalizing across everything. And the other was, you know, a few kinda wise people saying, you know, we need to find a way to pour more compute into these models at test time. We need to find a way to take what we had for kind of alpha go where you have a capable neural network, but then it becomes superhuman as you roll it out at scale and bring that to kind of language modeling, for example. And so our big pursuit over the past four years has been to find a way to build chips that will allow for kinda simultaneously taking these huge models and running them much, much, much faster than the chips of today, but do that in a way that kind of scales.

Speaker 1 | 02:21 - 02:29
So scales to models beyond the frontier today, scales to extraordinarily long contexts. And so that's the the mission that we've been on.

Speaker 2 | 02:29 - 02:41
It's become a much more interesting chip landscape in the four years since you started the company. Where would you place yourself in the overall GPU and accelerator landscape for inference?

Speaker 1 | 02:41 - 02:59
Yeah. It's a... There's a kind of extraordinary zoo now of options available. And if you look across this kind of entire space of kind of AI a six, one of the things that I think is very striking is there's a lot of relatively identikit chips out there. And this is kind of a structural...

Speaker 1 | 02:59 - 04:11
It's a kind of structural industry property where if you look especially across kind of hyperscaler efforts and, you know, Google kinda kicked this off with the TPU more than ten years ago, You see this paradigm where although there are a number of kind of proprietary internal chips, you know, Google with the TPU, Meta with MTIA, Microsoft with Maya, OpenAI now with Jalapeno, These chips that are ultimately developed and delivered in partnership with kind of a relatively small number of what we might call ASIC houses, these kind of back end delivery houses. Broadcom is is the largest, you know, $2,000,000,000,000 company that help people kind of realize these designs. And so when you kind of zoom into this this sort of seeming embarrassment of riches in the spectrum of what exists today, you see that actually there's a lot of similarity across these platforms. You know, all of these chips, you have HBM, this type of DRAM memory that is, you know, common to NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, and all of these other ASICs. You have the same kinds of bets on Tensor Cores to do your matrix multiplications, the same advanced packaging with TSMC.

Speaker 1 | 04:12 - 04:56

I think one thing that is notable about, you know, the dynamic between a chip vendor and a frontier lab, you know, if you look at Fractal, we try to be as aligned as possible with the needs of the frontier. We try to look a bit like some of those teams as well. We have people that really think deeply about these workloads and so on.

Speaker 1 | 33:58 - 34:32
So one of the cases that I think we sometimes need to make is explaining why we believe that over, you know, multiple decades, the world sustains some kind of frontier third party chip players. You know? Why does this not just roll up into these into these labs? And I think that comes down to the kind of asymmetric game that all of these labs and Frontier players have to play where they're exposed to an enormous risk if they go all in on a hardware bet. Suppose I'm, you know, I'm lab one, and I've gone all in on some proprietary silicon.

Speaker 1 | 34:33 - 35:00
And then lab two discovers some new computational breakthrough that delivers far better computational efficiencies for the same level of intelligence, but it only works on the chip that they've decided to deploy. I could die in the nine months before I get to deploy enough of that chip that I've also now gained that kind of five x in computational efficiency. And so there is a really urgent need for these chips to actually deploy the same... These companies to deploy the same platforms as one another. They're playing different games.

Speaker 1 | 35:00 - 35:14
Right? They're trying to now compete, you know, in the model where I think having deeply differentiated bets and going all in on those differentiated bets at the chip player is sort of an irrational and a very dangerous move for anybody that is playing at the frontier.

Speaker 2 | 35:14 - 35:17
Well, I think that's a great place to end. Thanks so much, Walter.

Speaker 1 | 35:17 - 35:18
Thanks very much, Sarah.

Speaker 2 | 35:20 - 35:37
